utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber has thoroughly considered the observations made yesterday by Mr. Piletta-Zanin and unanimously considers that the trial proceeds in the same spirit of neutrality and impartiality as expected from professional judges as it did before. The Chamber is of the opinion that the parties are free to exercise all procedural rights granted them by the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Mr. Mundis, is the Prosecution ready to continue its cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, shortly before we broke yesterday, I described to you a process that we're going to go through this morning with respect to the notes and interviews that you conducted. And I told you that we had been provided with photocopies of your notes and that there were certain portions of those notes which our language assistants had a difficult time in deciphering your handwriting. What I'm going to do now, with the assistance of the usher, is to provide to you a bundle of the handwritten notes and ask you to assist us with respect to the material that you've written on the notes. Do you understand what I'm asking you to do, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would also ask that -- if Madam Usher could put the material on the ELMO at the time when I indicate, it might be helpful so that everyone can follow exactly what it is the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if you could place the first stapled section of that material on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, one of the individuals that you spoke with was Visnja Stojanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not Visnja Stojanovic. It's General Stojanovic, commander during the war of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the notes that are on the ELMO to your right and indicate if the notes that you have before you are the notes you took when you interviewed General Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please turn to tab number 1, which is ERN number 01189428 in the original and page 14 of the English translation. You'll see, witness, there's a tab with the number "1." If you could please place that back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if the ELMO could be zoomed back or the document raised that the highlighted portion is visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see in the margin a blue highlight. Can you please read that portion of your notes next to the blue highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask you to do it slowly so that the interpreters and transcribers can follow you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This part of my notes relates to snipers. I'm reading from the top. "In every section according to establishment one sniper before the war." Item 2 -- can I go on? Second bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please indicate on the first line where it says "before the war."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "One sniper before the war." The last two words "pre rata," in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And second bullet, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sniping rifles introduced but there were not many. Serbs abandoned lines if they had sniping rifles."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the bullets underneath that, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an explanation of what kind of sniper rifles we're talking about. "Semi-automatic rifle," that's the first bullet. Next bullet: "Not even needed because everything was within the range of firearms." Following bullet: "In the second half of the war, this need became greater." I can't read the next line because it has been cut off in this copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. These portions of your notes were referring to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. If we could then go to the second stapled bundle of the notes, please. Witness, you also interviewed Cedo Sladoje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what position did he hold during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he was in the staff of the Territorial Defence, as far as I know. And during the war, he was chief of the operations department of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you please turn to tab 2, ERN number 01189445 in the original, pages 38 and 39 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said 445. I have "444" here. Is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can see the document, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if you could look, please, at bullet number 6 again with the blue highlighted portion to the right -- or to the left of that number 6. Can you please read out the highlighted portion beginning with bullet point number 6.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 6: "Sniping. According to establishment, every sniper's section -- so according to establishment, every sniper's section. Assignments issued by section commander." Second bullet: "Groups of snipers. It is the platoon commander who issues assignments."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Keep going, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The corps ordered the setting up of sniping units. Warnings issued against the danger of hostile snipers and the organising of anti-sniping sections." Following bullet: "Training of snipers." Following bullet: "7.9-millimetre sniper, 7.62 PAP, semi-automatic rifle with sniper." Following bullet: "12.7-millimetre snipers. We didn't have them in 1994. We only got them from the Muslims at the end of 1994. We used rifles with optical sights." That's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, again, this section of your notes is referring to sniping within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the second half of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Bullet number 7, can you please read that out for us.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The MUP had 12.7-millimetre snipers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me just briefly return to point 6. You indicated -- or the notes indicate in the first line "according to establishment." When was that? What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- that relates to the second half of 1994, when we started establishing anti-sniper units for anti-sniping activities. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the latter half of 1994. In mid-1994 we didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's not what the notes say though is it, witness?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here. You see in the middle --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The only reference in these notes with respect to the end of 1994 has to do with 12.7-millimetre rifles. The bullets above that say nothing about end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right. You have to know the context, the background. This item, this bullet which says that the corps formed anti-sniping units -- will you please let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just -- I'll give you an opportunity to finish, but let me just ask you in the first bullet under paragraph 6, where is there a reference to 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about the background, the linking up of anti-sniping units within the context of anti-sniping activities from August, when the corresponding agreement has been reached. So the corps has ordered the forming of snipers units by brigades. Not in a single document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Will you see a reference to an anti-sniping unit before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the first bullet of paragraph 6 of your notes, there is no reference to 1994, is there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, again, I understand that you want to place it in context. My question is very simple: In the first bullet under paragraph number 6, is there in your handwritten notes a reference to 1994; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reference to either 1992 or 1993 either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you about any notes and deciphering them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you also interviewed Marko Lugonja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Marko Lugonja told you that the SRK was disbanded after Dayton and the documents were all over the place. Do you remember him saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I know that's the case. And whether it's Marko Lugonja who told me that, I would have to look up my notes to see that. But I know that this fact is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, who was Marko Lugonja or who is Marko Lugonja?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Lugonja is a general. He was chief of the intelligence and security section in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps -- or rather, he was assistant corps commander for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, witness, the military regulations require the archiving of military records and documents, do they not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am not an employee of the archives, but I know that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And documents -- primary documents would have been a very important source for you in making your report. And I'm asking you what inquiries you made concerning the corps documents to the Defence legal team.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not an investigator, nor was I involved in the search for documents. I was given documents by the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you make any inquiries concerning documents, or did you make any inquiries in order to obtain documents that you didn't have?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I always insisted that documents be made available to me, especially documents I was missing and I still miss, such as documents issued by the Supreme Command of the BH army to their own staff and to their own units. Those are the documents that I didn't have. And I think it was a great handicap for both my report and for the entire proceedings, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to focus your attention on SRK documents. What steps did you take independently of those documents that the Defence provided to you to search for or obtain the important missing documents that were crucial for you to prepare your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look for any documents. I received all the documents that were essential for me. And the documents that the Defence provided me with for the SRK were quite relevant and sufficient for me to view what the situation was and to write a report that was relevant, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I suggest to you, witness, that the SRK documents, had they been properly collected, catalogued, and archived, that your task as an expert and the task that this Trial Chamber is undertaking would have been easier - isn't that right - had these documents before properly collected and archived?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not an affair of mine or of the Defence's. It's a matter of the archives. The units were disbanded. They would lose the archives, you know, when the army is transformed, when units are disbanded, the political and strategic situation changes, it's different. And in such cases there are failures, failings that occur. And this isn't a matter for me or the Defence, and this is something we can discuss: Were these documents I had sufficient for me to write a report? I think that they were, but I didn't have documents from the other side which are available for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in your report you allude to the fact that there are SRK documents that you would have liked to have reviewed but the documentation was not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'll withdraw that, Mr. President. Mr. President, could we be provided with a reference for the report so that we can check this, because I think that it was stated that he regretted not having documents but not only of those belonging to the SRK but other documents too. So if I could be provided with the page reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Mr. President, and perhaps we'll return to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The disbanding of a unit such as a corps is hardly a satisfactory explanation for the non-existence of an archive, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking me about. That's not a question that I should answer. But if you really want me to -- well, I don't think it's good for archives to be lost, to be closed down. Archives constitute part of history, and I think that this is a pity. But don't ask me how this happened or why this happened. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the question is simply whether or not the fact that the corps was disbanded was a good reason for not archiving the corps's documents. Is that a good reason, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an academic question whether it's a good reason or not. We should see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should try and determine why this was done. I don't know. But whether it's a good reason or not, it's not a reason at all. Disbanding a corps is not a reason to destroy the archives disbanding the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think this goes beyond the scope of General Radinovic's competence as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, one could wonder whether it does or not. But since the witness has answered the question, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Simply, for the record, Mr. President, the witness told us his doctoral dissertation is in the methodology of military science, and that would seem to go right to the issue of maintaining military records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I suggest to you that the SRK archives were intentionally dismembered and dispersed. What is your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. The relevance of the question with regard to the matter that we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is -- I think also this question has been answered by the witness, that he says he doesn't know. But the objection based on relevance is rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I would ask now with the assistance of the usher that we turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I don't know if we will carry on and follow this line, but the objection also concerns the chronological time frame. These events took place after what we are interested in, after September 1994. If we're talking about the disbanding of the Romanija Corps and as a result of the archives and also of the loss of the archives, the voluntary loss of the archives, all of this happened a long time after the relevant time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Of major relevance for the sources still available for the experts to reconstruct or to give us their opinion on what happened in the time before. I mean, the mere fact that disbanding a corps took place later, it even, I would say, from a logical point of view, that would be no case if the SRK would have been disbanded during or before that time. So it's certainly relevant, although mainly on the basis of sources available for experts to base their opinion upon. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask now with the assistance of the usher that we turn to what's marked as tab 4 in the witness's notes. And perhaps the witness could be shown the first page to indicate who these notes refer to. So if you could place just the first page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what you now have before you are the notes of your interview with Marko Lugonja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please turn to the tab number 4. In order to save time, we're skipping tab 3. Go to tab 4, please. This is ERN page number 01189449 and page 45 in the English translation. If you could -- again to save time, ignore the highlighted portion at the top and turn to the bottom of that page where there are two lines indicated with the blue highlighter. Can you please read for us the two lines that have been highlighted at the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "General Lugonja said --" and I wrote this down" -- the snipers weren't special units. They were part of units. They were within units. The commander of the battalion and company issued tasks to snipers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And witness, this -- these two sentences refer to snipers within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mundis. Which is the English page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe -- it's page 45, I believe. You've found it, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, these two sentences refer to snipers within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this corps, the units of the corps -- there's the corps it's an organisational establishment structure, and it can have its units. But here it says that the corps didn't have units, so the snipers didn't form a special unit. They didn't form a unit, but the snipers -- it was a military occupational specialty that existed within the units. And as they were important, commanders of companies and battalions issued them with tasks and they said which important military targets the snipers should target. These were observations, couriers, targetsmen. These were military targets, and the purpose of snipers is to fire at such targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, again, in order to save time I would ask if you could please focus on the questions I'm asking. My question was: These two sentences refer to snipers in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to [Realtime transcript read in error "two"] snipers in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I would now ask that you turn to the -- to the notes of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be some confusion. The answer was: "Yes, to snipers in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps." But it appears in the transcript as "T-W-O" as I understood it to be "T-o."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask that the witness be shown -- I would ask if they could please -- I'm hearing audible noises, Mr. President, from the Defence bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask now that the witness be shown the bundle that includes tab number 6 -- or excuse me, number 5, the bundle with tab number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry. I was trying to reread the transcript. There are a lot of omissions in this transcript. We would have to -- I'd have to discuss with Mrs. Pilipovic. And if I hear comments that I can hear the Defence, well, we've left school a long time ago. Things are going very fast. We can't listen to the witness, concentrate on what the Prosecution is saying, try to find the errors and do all this in silence as if we were telepathic. I don't have such a talent, contrary to the Prosecution without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Time will be given to that. And if I may make a suggestion, whenever you keep your earphones on, as I see Ms. Pilipovic does, you need a louder voice to understand. So as long as one of you two conferring keeps his headphones on, the automatic consequence will be that the -- that the other person has to speak louder in order to be understood. So therefore, if you take off your earphones while conferring, it will certainly assist in keeping the level of noise down. General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall make sure that I take my headphones off next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking about Ms. Pilipovic. General Galic, you're --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we have a problem with the microphone. It doesn't seem to be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see it's -- its light is on at this moment. General Galic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are conferring, rather not do it with the microphone on. Yes, now it functions. Was there anything you would like to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to confer, Mr. President, after all of these statements. Could you please allow me to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Give you an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't finished, Mr. President. And so as not to make any noise and bother the Prosecution, I will check the transcript in silence. Thank you. Yes, Mr. President. The objection is that it seems that we're talking about two different levels. The witness spoke about units when he provided his answer in Serb, in the Serbian language, and the question that followed in relation to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps this should be done in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Madam Usher, to escort the witness out of the courtroom for a second. General Radinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, I understood the last question to be whether it was within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps or within any other corps. And if there would be any doubt as to that, we could easily clarify that. I do understand that the witness said that snipers were located in the units and not directly related to the corps command but under the command of the units. If that's the issue, I think we could clarify that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But it should be said that what we hear directly in the language of Shakespeare, that is, the language used by Mr. Mundis, is not necessarily what the witness hears. He does not necessarily understand the same thing. So confusion might arise in the witness's mind, and this immediately -- this is shared by General Galic and my colleague, so I think that the witness could be confused too. In other words, what I'm saying is that the witnesses given by the witness concern the level of the units themselves, and the development of the question as it was understood by Mrs. Pilipovic in her mother tongue might make one thing that one is referring to a superior, higher level, the level of the corps, and this is of considerable importance given the duties of the accused. So I think that if this matter was clarified and we were said that you're talk about units but these units of the Romanija Corps, in such a case things would be a lot clearer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the answers of the witness, I took it that he was not that confused, that he was able to correct if there was any misunderstanding. But we'll ask the witness. And Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Radinovic, when you told us about snipers within the units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, finally a question was put to you by Mr. Mundis saying that whether you're referring to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, that is - at least that's how I understood it - units within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. And when you said yes, it related to that, did you then intend to say to the units within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and not in another corps? Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try to understand the difference between the units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's perfectly clear. But none of your answers related to anything outside the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; is that a correct understanding? Not the Drina Corps or whatever other corps. You understood the questions to be about what happened within the corps at whatever level of units, platoons, or brigades, or -- that's how you understood the questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But so that things are clear, the item that we read out does not refer to sniper units under the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps because there were no such units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's perfectly clear. There seems to be no confusion any more. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, I would ask with the assistance of the usher that the witness be shown those portions of his notes that contain tabs 5, 6, and 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor said that I would help him to interpret some things that he wasn't able to read, and it appears that these questions don't refer to that aspect but to what he read, what he has understood, and what he wants to -- and he wants to impose his understanding of these things on me. But there is something that I would like to request too, and it's of a general nature: Since we are dealing with notes that I took in the course of my discussions, and I didn't take all the necessary precautions that one would take if you were writing official documents, would you allow me to check how they read what I wrote down, and they think that they read it correctly. Because I've already seen that the context of my notes has been changed, and this could have a certain effect. This could influence the way these notes are understood. And if this is going to be a document that will be discussed in the course of testimony and that will be given value as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution is inviting you to read those parts where they have difficulties either in reading, I take it, or understanding what you exactly did write down. And of course the Chamber is fully aware that short notes are not a verbatim record of your interview and only point to some issues you thought sufficiently relevant to write them down in brief words. And therefore, if there would be any need to further explain, as you did before, when you said the -- something happened only after 1994. If there is any such explanation needed in order to not distort the meaning of what you did write down, you can give that after you have answered the questions of the Prosecution. And if there's any doubt as to whether there's a correct reading, I think that is remedied by asking you to read out those parts of your notes. So if there's any need for you to explain, please ask me and I'll give you an opportunity to do so. But usually first answer the questions and then explain if there seems to be any misunderstanding in the way the question is put to you. On the other hand, I have to inform you that of course both parties are seeking to establish what they think is of importance for the presentation of their case. So there will be a difference between Defence and Prosecution in this respect. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the document could please again be placed with the front page to indicate whom the witness was speaking to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It appears, witness, at the top, above the number - and again this is ERN 01189450 - it appears that the name Makso is written. Is that what that says at the top?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not Makso. It's Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Marko. So again, this would be Marko Lugonja that you were interviewing on this day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Lugonja on several occasions, but I'm not sure that that was on the same day. I think that it actually wasn't on the same day, because the rhythm with which this was written is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The question was: These notes refer to an interview you conducted with Marko Lugonja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please turn to tab 5 of these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This, Mr. President, is on page 46 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You will see at the top, include the part where the staple is on this document, two lines, both beginning with "Josipovic." Can you please read out the top three lines, that is, the top two bullets, on the page before you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading. "Josipovic did not report on the problem with Vaske. He was loyal to him, Vaske. The symbol this Vaske wore was a skull with a helmet. That's the Vaske that the general had problems with. Next bullet: "Josipovic was more in the power of politics than the army."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And witness, who is Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Josipovic was an officer in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. He was the commander of the Ilijas Brigade, and on several occasions he was also commander of the Vogosca Tactical Group when the Vogosca Tactical Group was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have a transcript problem, Mr. President. I didn't listen to the English version. I don't know this -- if this was translated or not in the English version, but it seems to me that in the Serbian text there is a reference to UN -- sorry, a reference to the N, 4N. I don't know if it is in the transcript or not. Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see on the screen, that's the last two elements of the second line of the -- of the document? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly that. It's that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- General Radinovic, on the second line, it seems something like "4N" or "NN" or -- I cannot -- could you please tell us precisely what that stands for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that this Vaske used to wear a UN helmet with a skull drawn on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin, "4N" is still not -- I do not know what word --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It's UN. It's not 4N. It's UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Instead of 4N.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a United Nations helmet, UN helmet, a helmet of an UNPROFOR member. That's what this Vaske was wearing, with a skull painted on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I do understand. It was a UN helmet but something else painted on it. Then -- thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In order to save time if we could now turn to tab 7, which is ERN page numbers 01189455, and page 51 in the English translation. Witness, again, in order to save time, I'm only going to ask you to read the first major bullet and then the four smaller bullets underneath that. If you could please do that beginning with the very first bullet -- actually, start with the title that that covers, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Snipers." That's what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First bullet: "PAP." That's an abbreviation for a semi-automatic rifle. "7.62 and 7.9 millimetres."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Continue reading, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First subbullet: "This most of all, more than anything else, but a small number."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can hardly read this third subbullet. I think it says "not developed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you're having a difficult time reading your notes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, precisely. It's really difficult for me to read my own notes because during the interview I wrote this as a reminder. It wasn't drawn up as a document. Then fourth subbullet: "From the depot --" it says something like "hunting weapons." And the last subbullet says "untrained." Shall I read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the fourth subbullet, the one with "depots," does that also indicate sniper rifles, sniper rifles from depots?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I really can't read it. "From the depot, snipers were stolen to be used as hunting weapons," or "sniper rifles were stolen as hunting weapons." I can't read any better than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I think in order to save time, that's all we'll be doing with the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, Madam Usher, if you could please retrieve all of the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, witness, next I'd like to show you a document which was one of the documents that was attached or filed with your report. There were, as you know, about 130 documents that were filed with your expert report. You reviewed all of those documents that were filed and attached -- or attached to and filed with your report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would ask that this document be placed before the witness. We do have sufficient copies. This was premarked as Defence 259; however, it doesn't seem to have been tendered. We have clean copies without the D number on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if you could please place that document on the ELMO so that we can all see what it is you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Madam Usher has helped us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to read out loud the second paragraph of this document, the paragraph beginning "Svima nama".

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We all care about liquidating as many Turkish converts as possible but not at the cost of such political consequences as are caused by shells or grenades falling on Sarajevo with minimum effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And witness, this document was issued by the deputy commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This order was delivered according to the delivery line to all commands of SRK brigades and PKM; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That document can be returned to the usher. Witness, I'd now like to turn to that portion of your report where you discuss the accused, General Galic. How long have you known the accused for?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him very well personally. Perhaps we saw each other a couple of times when he visited schools. But I don't know him personally. We just know of each other. We are almost the same generation. He is four years younger. We knew of each other, as I said, but we were not friends and we don't know each other well enough so that I can give you some information about him that is not reflected in documents or in other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you were preparing your report, witness, did you speak to General Galic? Did you interview him or speak to him about preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, as the commander of the military police in Ljubljana for several years, the accused would have had a thorough understanding and knowledge of military law and disciplinary matters. In this capacity, you would have expected that he would have been thoroughly familiar with the military criminal justice system by the time that he arrived at the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the criminal legal system is not within the competence of the military police, and I would not be expected to be very familiar with criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the question is not necessarily whether the military police controlled the military criminal justice system. But as a commander of a military criminal police unit, he certainly would have had familiarity with military law, would he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than an average -- than an officer of average education. Military police has its own job. It doesn't deal with criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How would the military police be in a position to enforce the law if they don't know what the law is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military police receives assignments, assignments that are very specific, assignments to search, to take into custody, to keep territory under control, to protect the command post, to organise patrols, to protect checkpoints. That's what the police does. And if the prosecutor orders the police to take someone into custody, they comply. They don't ask whether the prosecutor is right or not, or the investigative judge or whoever it is that issues such warrants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In your opinion --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I know about it. That's as much as I know. You're asking me if I'm familiar with this. I'm really not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: According to your report, witness, and in your opinion I believe it's fair to say that you've written that the accused had a stellar military career. He served as a member of Tito's escort battalion. You characterise that as being indicative that he had joined the elite of the JNA, and you wrote that that indicated early in his career that he was destined for senior command. Is that a fair characterisation of the information in your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, witness, based on the interviews that you conducted, would you say that the accused was well liked and well respected among his subordinates and his senior subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have much less information about this than you could have heard from witnesses that testified in defence of General Galic. They gave you their views and judgments about him. I didn't ask his subordinates what they thought of him because it is simply indecent for a person outside their circle, outside their units, to ask such questions about the commander. It would be contrary to military ethics to ask questions about the commander of his subordinates, and I refrained from asking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on the research done in conducting your report to include the interviews that you conducted, is it fair to say, based on what you've read and the information that came into your possession, that the accused demanded high standards from himself and from his corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you say again, based on the research and information that came into your possession in compiling your report, that the accused was respected by members of his corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is difficult to conclude from these documents. All I know from the documents is that the command system did function. That is an indicator of their relationship between the commander and the subordinates and vice versa. Also in my report and in my earlier testimony I spoke about impeding factors that were present in General Galic's command system, from higher politic, UNPROFOR, media, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the question was a relatively straightforward one: Based on the information that you reviewed, the documents, the interviews, et cetera, was the corps commander respected by his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apart from certain exceptions, yes, he was held in very high regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, given the training, experience, these high standards that he held, and this respect that he garnered from his troops, if- and I stress here the word "if" - if the accused were to be convicted of the charges for which he faces, that finding would be all the more reprehensible because of his standing and position. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. I really tried to follow, but I couldn't understand. If you could be -- put it more briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. And I want to formulate -- to express my objection in the absence of the witness, unless Mr. Mundis wants to withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We do not want to withdraw the question. And I would ask that the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm reading here, Mr. President, in the language of Falstaff, that the term "reprehensible". What matters, in fact, what implies a strictly ethical notion. It's not a fact. It's a value judgment, to know whether the conduct of a certain individual was reprehensible or not and at the same time - this is the second level - also in the language of Othello, if you say would this make the charges against General Galic even worse. Now you are putting the witness in a situation when he is no longer able to testify about facts that he knows of but he's made to talk about things that he only can know by inference. This is a whole scene that should not be allowed to be played out here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will interpret that as being an objection on the grounds of relevance. Certainly it's relevant in the sense that the Prosecution has an obligation to put before the Trial Chamber any evidence that might go to a sentence in the event the accused were to be convicted. I stressed in my question if, I repeated that word twice. The question goes to the issue of sentencing and what we are trying to establish is in light of the accused's experience, reputation, training, and background as set forth by this witness in his report and in his testimony, whether or not that would be a particularly -- those -- the accused's background would be relevant to sentencing. And the Prosecution position would be in effect, to use a metaphor, "the bigger they are, the harder they fall," in the sense that as a senior commander with an outstanding record, if he were to be convicted, that that would be particularly reprehensible. And that's what the question goes to. It's an issue with respect to sentencing. And the Prosecution feels that under the Rules we are obligated to do this in light of the fact that we do not have bifurcated sentencing procedures before this Tribunal. And that's the relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, briefly. The Prosecution is confusing witness and Judges. Here is a question that should interest a Judge or Judges but not the witness. To know what is the degree of guilt of someone, supposing such guilt exists, that's not a question for the witness. And to ask it in such a manner amounts to badgering the witness -- perhaps not badgering, but putting him in a very sensitive situation. And it is this attitude, quasi-psychological treatment, that we object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, this is important evidence, the Prosecution submits, because one of the things that the Trial Chamber might have recourse to in the event the accused was to be convicted would be information concerning community standards with respect to sentence. This witness comes from in effect the same community that the accused does, and his views, therefore, would be particularly probative and relevant with respect to a sentence. That's why we're leading this evidence -- or that's why we're seeking to lead this evidence, Mr. President. It doesn't -- we're not asking this witness questions about guilt or innocence. We're simply asking him that in the event the accused were to be found guilty, how he would characterise or how he would view that in light of the accused's background experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. There is the facts the Prosecution would like to draw the attention to have been dealt with in previous questions, and their very last question does not assist the Chamber in making determinations, if the Chamber will have to do so. Therefore, we -- I'll ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the time, I was going to suggest that perhaps now would be a time for a break, in light of the fact that there's -- the following subjects will require quite a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then adjourn -- I'm sorry for you, General, that we asked you to come back and then adjourn at that same moment. We'll adjourn until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, just a couple of follow-up questions from prior to the break. You testified on the 7th of March about the accused. And as part of that testimony, there was some fine detail about his personal circumstances, including issues related to his family situation. You've told us that you didn't interview the accused. How is it that it came into your possession this -- these details concerning the accused's family situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Banja Luka on a study trip, and I visited Mrs. Galic. I spoke to her, and these are things that I found out from speaking to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, where in your report do you indicate that Mrs. Galic was a source of information that you relied upon in producing your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you don't think I should have mentioned that Mrs. Galic told me that she had information of any kind that was important for my report. You just asked me how I was familiar with the family background, and this is not a matter I dealt with in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But you certainly included information that you received from Mrs. Galic in your report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It was a visit which I -- which was a matter of courtesy. I went to Banja Luka with the Defence, and we visited the family as a matter of courtesy, and I listened to what she had to say and there were certain things that I knew about in any case, as an informed officer, a well-informed officer, I knew most of the officers from our army, and it's quite simply something that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, witness, you've told us now here today that you spoke to Mrs. Galic. Is that -- in Banja Luka. You've told us that just now. Where in your report do you specify the information that you obtained from Mrs. Galic in producing this report? Where do you cite to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could I be allowed not to answer questions that don't have to do with the subject that we are discussing. I visited Mrs. Galic as a matter of courtesy. I wasn't alone, and we didn't discuss anything that might be relevant to this trial. Don't ask me to remember and to improvise, because these are conversations that are quite customary when you visit someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course there's nothing against visiting Mrs. Galic. But when you're asked what was the source of your knowledge of family details and you describe a few family details in your report, your answer was "I went to Banja Luka on a study trip and I visited Mrs. Galic. I spoke to her, and these are things that I found out from speaking to her." So what you said is that these family details, that you knew about them on the basis of a conversation, even if it was a matter of courtesy that you visited Mrs. Galic, on the basis of a conversation with Mrs. Galic. The only thing the Prosecution at this moment seems to do is to explore whether all the sources - and you just indicated that this was a source in this respect - are written down in your report being the source of your information. That's what the Prosecution asked you about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information that we have just exchanged, these aren't things that I mentioned in the report, and therefore I was under no obligation to mention this as a source. I don't know why this matter being addressed. But if it is really important, I'm quite ready to discuss this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's not a matter of major importance, as a matter of fact, but you testified yourself that the family details you did write down in your report, that you learnt them from Mrs. Galic. That's four minutes ago, it was you yourself who testified that this was your source, and then the next question was why this source was not mentioned in the report. But I don't know whether it's of major importance to further explore this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during your military career, have you ever personally been in combat?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So it would equally be true that you've never commanded troops in a combat situation.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in a combat situation. I've been involved in training in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said "fortunately, I have not been involved in combat".

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to turn now to the second half of your report, pages 101 through 195. In this part of your report, you provide an in-depth analysis of the charges against the accused. And in reaching these conclusions, you relied on all the sources listed at the beginning of your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it is. But if you ask me about some specific source, I'd be able to provide you with a more concrete answer. But you can only answer a general question in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as part of the process of reaching your conclusions, you considered all the material together and assessed the credibility of the material and weighed the relative weights to be given to all this material. You did all of these things so that your report would be objective. Is that a fair summary of what you've done?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how you proceed in general. If someone uses sources, the sources that are considered to be relevant are selected. Various sources have varying kinds of value, as information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, witness, would you consider that the role that you have undertaken in this case is one of being an independent expert?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that's equally true of the role that you played in both the Foca and Krstic cases as well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I strive to be independent. My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself to be biased in any way with respect to the parties to the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us that you've reviewed tens of thousands of pages of documents. Based on your analysis of these documents and the other sources that you relied upon, would you say that the conclusions in your report are definitive?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question. What do you mean when you say "definitive"? It was translated as "definitive." I don't know if that is what you said. It was translated as "final."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on the documents that you've reviewed and the other source material, are the conclusions that you've reached in your opinion conclusive? Are they definitive?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene at this point, and I'm doing this out of respect for everyone. It's possible that the witness might be troubled, but I have to say this in front of him because contrary to what you said, Mr. President, a minute ago, the Prosecution did not ask why -- didn't want to find out why this witness did not mention the sources or, rather, Mrs. Galic, to whom he referred himself. The Prosecution only wanted to find or should only find out where these sources are mentioned in the report. And as these questions were put to the witness -- but perhaps he didn't understand the difference between the question of why asked by -- and where, which is the question asked by the Prosecution. Perhaps the witness is in a delicate situation. So in our opinion, there is an error -- the Prosecution isn't asking about why, it's asking about where in the text. And I think that the witness would feel at great ease if the question were put to him in this sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few minutes ago you were asked about mentioning your visit to Mrs. Galic as a source of your -- a source of your opinion. Later on I explained - and perhaps not for the full 100 per cent correct - the reason why these questions were put to you. There were no further questions put to you. When you were asked about mentioning the source, was there any confusion on your side as to the answer you would have to give to those answers -- to those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was confused seeing that in such serious proceedings that deal with such a serious subject such as the war in the Sarajevo theatre, I was confused by the fact that certain matters were being investigated that had to do with events that concern courtesy, which are matters of courtesy. I can see some pretty ladies in front of me, but these aren't sources of information that I would mention. I'm quite relaxed. Now I can answer any question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. Were you confused on the issue I just mentioned to you? Was there any other confusion, apart from the one you have mentioned, that you thought that more important matters would be the subject of debate in this court? Was there any other confusion, as far as the questions are concerned? I mean, would you have answered those questions in a different way? I think, as a matter of fact, that -- no. Would you have answered these questions in a different way depending on whether the Prosecution would like to establish whether you did not mention them or why you didn't mention them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer any questions put to me by the Prosecution to the extent that I have knowledge about such matters. When I went to see Mrs. Galic, I didn't go there to investigate anything, and this was not a source of information for my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went with the Defence to pay her a visit, when I was on my study trip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Radinovic, yes, you're repeating now what you say, which contradicts your own testimony. But -- then perhaps your testimony is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still don't understand what the sense of the question is. I still don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then let me -- do you have to make -- you've now explained why you did not mention your visit to Mrs. Galic as a source in your report. That's clear. Is there anything else to be clarified?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I just wanted to clarify this issue, and I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you've reviewed tens of thousands of pages of documents and you've had recourse to other sources as well. On the basis of all of these materials that you've reviewed, would you say that in your report you have clearly demonstrated that the accused is not guilty of the charges for which he's accused?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you would testify here today that you found no evidence that he was responsible for the sniping and shelling of the civilian population in Sarajevo or no evidence that the accused was responsible for terrorising the civilian population of the city of Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in producing your report, did you consider any evidence that might contradict the position advanced by the accused? And if you did, can you please cite us to a page or paragraph in your report where you acknowledge the truth of any of that contradictory evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object because the question is in fact so complicated, if we bear in mind the structure of the indictment and the reference to Article 3 or 7, and it would require the competence of a legal expert. And perhaps General Radinovic does not have this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last question put to the witness is not something that would need legal expertise. The question to you was whether there -- where to find in your report reference to evidence that contradicts your findings, just by giving an example of such a place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My report consists of 200 pages, and it would be difficult for me now to find the references that the Prosecution has asked for. But I did analyse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not asking you to give the full -- and the Prosecution doesn't ask you to give the full set of where you made reference to evidence that contradicts the position of the Defence but to just -- as an indication to give one or several examples of where you paid specifically attention to evidence that would be contrary to the evidence presented by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my report, I analysed the operative positions of the parties involved in the conflict, and in that part of the analysis I discussed the thesis that appears in the indictment and in supplementary material and in testimonies of witnesses and in other secondary material that deals with the Sarajevo Romanija Corps at all elevated positions around Sarajevo. And by using the map and video cassettes and in my report, I contested this thesis by referring to specific empirical facts that I established when investigating the matter for this testimony. And if we are discussing the weapons that the parties in the conflict had, it's also possible to find in my report a part that mentions the fact that it is not correct to claim that the 1st BH army Corps was not armed and that in Sarajevo there was only the civilian population and not the army. I have presented before this Trial Chamber and I have also mentioned this in my report, I have mentioned a lot of documents which show that the entire city of Sarajevo was an enormous military target. The commander of the 1st BH army Corps has also testified here and a commander of one of his brigades, an expert, a shelling expert, and they all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You're not -- you're not answering the question. You're now explaining to us on the basis of what circumstances you find the indictment to be incorrect. The question, however, was a totally different one. The question was: Where in your report evidence that would contradict the Defence positions - and you referred now to evidence that would support the Defence positions - where such evidence can be found in your report. So evidence that, I would say, would be in favour of the Prosecution and against the Defence rather than the other way around, where to find that in the report. That's the question to you. And just give a few examples of that. That's what the Prosecution asked you to do. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I based my report above all on documents. I said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was asking the same thing as the witness. He should be allowed to refer to his report because he has to answer on the basis of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was no need to intervene at this very moment. Could you answer, whether by referring to your report, whether you could do it by heart. If you would need your report, then please ask for a copy if you haven't got one so that you can refer to the pages. But could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the documents from the BH army 1st Corps contain information and mentioned facts that support the Prosecution's thesis. Part of the documents or some of the facts referred to in those documents which I have mentioned here support the Defence. So none of the documents that I referred to, none of the documents from the archives of the 1st Corps of the BH army, are documents which fully support the Defence thesis. But to a large extent they support the Prosecution thesis. So I didn't select documents. I wasn't biased. I analysed the documents that presented the best overview of the military situation which would allow one to determine whether General Galic was responsible or not. If the responsibility of some other commander in the 2nd Corps was concerned, I would have reversed the situation. I would have analysed things differently. But we're dealing with the responsibility of General Galic and of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, so naturally one looks for facts that are for or against this, that support this thesis or deny it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I do understand your answer well, you say where I referred to documents of the 1st Corps, that's where you find in my report facts that contradict the Defence case and seem to support, at least to some extent, the Prosecution's case. That's a clear answer. That's where we find it in your report. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask that the witness be shown map 1913, Defence map 1913. It's not necessary to place it on the ELMO, usher. I just want to refresh the witness's recollection as to which map we're talking about. So as long as he's got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, looking at map D1913, it would appear that the city of Sarajevo is riddled with legitimate military targets in your opinion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And here it's [indiscernible] to an extent in comparison to what the actual situation was. There are far more targets, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in reality, there would be even more targets than are indicated on that map.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It would seem, witness, that if what you're saying is right, that any mortar, artillery, tank, triple A round, or any small arm fire that hit a civilian in the city could be explained away as having been intended for a legitimate military target but that the round went astray. Do you accept that? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object because the question as it stands is very general. It would be necessary to be more specific. It would be necessary to relate it to the presence of an attack, the absence of an attack, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, a further specification of the question would prevent answers that do not assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if -- you've told us that there were even more targets than you put on the map. You've told us that a couple of times. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you were to put all of the targets on that map, would there be any area at all in the city of Sarajevo that wasn't a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So based on your analysis of the information, the entire city of Sarajevo was a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A legitimate target was any place where there was -- where there were army troops, on the Serbian side and on the presidency side. That's the term that is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My question was a slightly different one: Based on your analysis of the information and what you've just told us, the entire city of Sarajevo would seem to be a legitimate military target in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. Since we're talking about the entire city of Sarajevo, does this also include Nedzarici, Grbavica, Ilijas, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would refer you in my LiveNote to page 44, line 5, the response which the witness gave. He certainly could have clarified that had he chosen to but did not do so. I would also note that the witness didn't seem to have any confusion with respect to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said that there would not be any area that would not -- on the map that wasn't a legitimate military target, I take it that you referred - but please tell me if I'm wrong - you referred to the area under the control of the BiH forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said - and I don't know if it's on the transcript - that anywhere where you have troops, both on the Muslim and the Serbian side, it is a legitimate military target. Where you have are military resources is a place that is a military target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was your next answer. But your first answer was -- you were asked. I'll read it literally to you:. Mr. Mundis said: "Witness --" no, let me just see. Yes. You were asked: "If you were to put all the targets on that map, would there be any area at all in the city of Sarajevo that wasn't a legitimate military target?" Your answer then was: "No, there wouldn't." Were you then referring to the BiH-controlled areas or to the other areas as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the entire city of Sarajevo, including Grbavica, including Nedzarici, Ilidza, Vogosca, because there were troops everywhere. Anywhere where you have troops is a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then putting military targets on the map, you restricted yourself to the BiH-controlled area, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Said that there would be more military targets than those indicated on the map, you referred to that same area on which you marked the military targets, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if you were asked about what would be the consequence of putting all military targets on the map, it seems logical that you're referring to that same area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I was referring to that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in reviewing the evidence of the specific scheduled sniping and shelling incidents, what evidence did you review in reaching the conclusions that the accused was not guilty of those offences?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I studied all of these incidents. I listened to testimony. I have studied all the documents. I have taken into account the military resources that were located in the part of Sarajevo for which General Galic is charged. And I came to the conclusion that Sarajevo was packed with military targets, that those targets were legitimate, and that the greatest suffering was incurred in exchanges of fire because it is absolutely natural to expect that if there is outgoing fire from the city, there would be a response. This is the conclusion reached from the information that was available to me. As for specific incidents, you had testimony on that, you had experts, and there was no reason for me to study them in particular, in addition to what they said here and what they have prepared for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
